extracted.intended_audience: patent attorneys, IP litigators, and practitioners handling EPO oppositions and appeals (and advanced students of European patent law)
extracted.subtask_description: Procedural and substantive standards governing opposition, appeal and Boards of Appeal practice before the European Patent Office, including grounds for opposition, admissibility and timing of submissions, amendment rules (the convergent approach), oral proceedings, evidence, representation, confidentiality and costs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds for opposition / revocation
rubrics_metrics.description: Opposition may only be filed on the grounds that the patent’s subject matter is not patentable (e.g., lack of novelty, lack of inventive step, excluded subject matter), that the patent does not disclose the invention clearly and completely for a person skilled in the art, or that the patent’s subject matter extends beyond the content of the earlier application as filed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These grounds are exhaustive under the EPC (art. 100). In opposition proceedings the Opposition Division examines whether the grounds prejudice maintenance of the patent and may invite written observations; proprietor may file amended description/claims/drawings but late-filed proposals may be disregarded.

rubrics_metrics.name: Nine-month opposition time limit
rubrics_metrics.description: A notice of opposition must be filed within nine months after the publication of the mention that a European patent has been granted.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If not filed within nine months, the centralized opposition remedy is foreclosed (EPC, art. 99(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Outcomes of opposition proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: At the conclusion of opposition proceedings, the Opposition Division may (i) reject the opposition and maintain the patent as granted; (ii) maintain the patent in amended form; or (iii) revoke the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Decisions have effect in all designated Contracting States; proprietor amendments during opposition must not extend protection conferred (art. 123(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Appeal filing deadlines and basic formal content
rubrics_metrics.description: An appellant must file a notice of appeal within two months of notification of the decision and a statement setting out the grounds of appeal within four months. The notice must identify the appellant, the decision impugned and a request defining the subject of the appeal; the statement must give reasons and the facts and evidence relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These time limits are mandatory (EPC, art.108; RPBA 2020). The respondent has four months to file a reply after notification of the grounds of appeal (RPBA 2020, art. 12(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Front‑loading / complete appeal case requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: The appellant’s statement of grounds of appeal and the respondent’s reply must contain each party’s complete appeal case.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This 'front‑loading' ensures the Board and rapporteur have all facts and requests at the outset. Because of this, later amendments are increasingly limited (RPBA 2020, art. 12(3)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Convergent approach to amendments of parties’ appeal cases
rubrics_metrics.description: As appeal proceedings progress, the possibilities for parties to amend their cases become increasingly limited; this convergent approach is structured in three levels under the RPBA 2020.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Which level applies depends on timing: (1) Article 12(4) — changes at outset in the statement of case; (2) Article 13(1) — changes after initial stage but before summons to oral proceedings; (3) Article 13(2) — changes after summons (usually very late), each with increasingly stringent admissibility criteria.

rubrics_metrics.name: First-level amendment admissibility (Article 12(4))
rubrics_metrics.description: If a party changes its case in its statement of case compared with what it filed before the first-instance division, the change is treated as an amendment and may be admitted only at the Board’s discretion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boards may consider complexity of the amendment, suitability to address issues underlying the decision under appeal, and procedural economy. Submissions not directed to the requests/facts/arguments on which the decision was based may be regarded as amendments. A party must also show that auxiliary requests or previously-filed items were maintained before the division if relevant (RPBA 2020, art. 12(4)–(6)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Second-level amendment admissibility (Article 13(1))
rubrics_metrics.description: When a party amends its appeal case after the initial exchange of briefs but before a summons to oral proceedings, amendments are subject to the Board’s discretion under stricter criteria than at the first level.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The party must give reasons why the initial case is amended only at this stage. The Board will consider whether the amendment is suitable to resolve the issues and whether it harms procedural economy. For patent amendments, the proprietor must demonstrate prima facie that the amendment overcomes objections and does not introduce new ones (RPBA 2020, art. 13(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Third-level amendment admissibility (Article 13(2))
rubrics_metrics.description: Once a summons to oral proceedings has been notified (or late after a Board-set period), amendments are generally not taken into account except in 'exceptional circumstances' where cogent reasons justify admission.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of exceptional circumstances include (rarely) a new objection first raised by the Board in its communication preparing the oral proceedings; the party must explain why the objection is new and provide compelling reasons (RPBA 2020, art. 13(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Admissibility requirements for statements of grounds and replies (clarity and completeness)
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements of grounds and replies must clearly and concisely set out why the decision should be reversed/amended/upheld and must expressly specify all requests, facts, objections, arguments and evidence relied upon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any part of submissions not meeting this requirement may be excluded (RPBA 2020, art. 12(3), (5)). Documents/requests already not admitted by the Opposition Division or which should have been submitted earlier may be excluded under art. 12(6).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on taking new evidence and amendments previously not considered at first instance
rubrics_metrics.description: A submission which was not addressed by the first instance because the division saw no need (e.g., auxiliary requests not considered) may still be treated as an amendment on appeal and the party must show it was admissibly raised before and maintained.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the party demonstrates admissible maintenance, the item cannot be excluded by the Board; otherwise it may be treated as a late amendment and possibly not admitted (RPBA 2020, art. 12(4)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Role and powers of the Boards of Appeal
rubrics_metrics.description: The Boards of Appeal are the first and final judicial instance within the EPO for review of contested decisions of departments of first instance, not bound by instructions, and must comply only with the EPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boards review points of law and fact, are specialized patent judiciary (typically two technical + one legally qualified member), and their decisions are final and persuasive domestically and internationally (EPC arts. 23(3), 106(1)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Enlarged Board of Appeal functions
rubrics_metrics.description: The Enlarged Board ensures uniform application of the EPC by deciding points of law referred by Boards of Appeal or the President; it also gives opinions where Boards have diverging decisions and performs a limited judicial review of Boards’ decisions for fundamental procedural defects.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a Board refers a point, the Enlarged Board decides only that point and the referring Board remains bound by that decision for the referred point. Petitions for review under art. 112a are exceptional and strictly limited (EPC art.112; RPBA references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Remittal and relationship with national courts and the UPC
rubrics_metrics.description: The EPO Boards, national courts of Contracting States and the Unified Patent Court have concurrent jurisdiction on validity; infringement falls to national courts and UPC.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A European patent revoked by the Boards may not be reinstated by national courts/UPC and vice versa; centralized opposition/appeal concerns the entire bundle of national parts (EPC arts. 99–101; Agreement on a Unified Patent Court).

rubrics_metrics.name: Case assignment and business distribution scheme
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical appeals are allocated to Technical Boards according to the business distribution scheme before each working year, primarily by main IPC class at time of appeal filing; chairs may reallocate for technical appropriateness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chairs consider technical and language requirements and workload. Boards that share IPC classes may split by year of appeal filing; the Presidium adopts and can amend the scheme (Business Distribution Scheme; RPBA references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Board composition rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Technical Boards usually have 4–8 technically qualified members and 2–4 legally qualified members; appeals are normally decided by a panel of two technical and one legal member.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Technical members are typically fixed to one Board, legal members to several. The chair determines specific composition taking into account technical/language needs and workloads (EPC, r.12b; Business Distribution Scheme).

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation requirements (professional representatives)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties are not generally obliged to be represented by a professional representative, but if they do not have residence or principal place of business in a Contracting State they must be represented by a professional representative and act through them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A professional representative must be a national of a Contracting State, have place of business or employment in a Contracting State, and have passed the European Qualifying Examination (EPC arts. 133–134; failure to appoint when required renders procedural steps by the non-represented party as not taken).

rubrics_metrics.name: Language of proceedings and interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Each case has a language of proceedings (English/German/French) determined by filing language; at oral proceedings parties may use any official EPO language but must give notice at least one month in advance for EPO-organised interpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Parties may provide their own interpretation at their expense; mixed-language oral proceedings with interpretation are frequent. Language choice affects organization and cost (EPC art.14(3); r.4).

rubrics_metrics.name: Right to oral proceedings and summons timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties have a right to oral proceedings; if requested by a party a hearing must be arranged. Parties are usually summoned at least four months before the hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If no party requests a hearing the Board may still summon the parties or decide in written proceedings. Requests to change date require serious reasons; oral proceedings are normally public but can be excluded in exceptional cases (EPC art.116; RPBA 2020, art.15).

rubrics_metrics.name: Boards’ communication in preparation for oral proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: The Boards always issue a communication in preparation for oral proceedings that draws attention to matters of particular significance and usually states a preliminary opinion on decisive points.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These communications are normally issued at least four months in advance and are intended to help parties focus; a new objection raised in such a communication can, in some cases, justify late amendments under exceptional circumstances (RPBA 2020, art.15).

rubrics_metrics.name: Oral proceedings by videoconference and mixed modes
rubrics_metrics.description: Oral proceedings may be held by videoconference in 'distributed' mode (all attend remotely) or 'mixed' mode (some attend in person, others remotely); in exceptional cases board members may attend remotely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These formats are permitted under RPBA 2020, art.15a; practical arrangements depend on case and participants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Decision announcement and written decision timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: Final decisions are usually announced at the end of oral proceedings; the written decision (summary of facts, reasons and order) must be despatched within three months of the oral proceedings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the Board cannot meet the three‑month deadline (e.g., sickness, complexity), it should inform the parties of the delay and expected dispatch date. The written decision is signed by the chair and registrar and is notified to all parties (RPBA 2020, art.15(9); EPC r.102).

rubrics_metrics.name: Abridged reasons for decision (conditions)
rubrics_metrics.description: A Board may present reasons for a decision in an abridged form only with the parties’ consent and provided no third party has a legitimate interest in full reasons; alternatively where the Board fully agrees with the findings of the decision under appeal.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: In practice, abridged reasons are rare; a Board cannot abridge reasons if a third party or court has expressed a legitimate interest in full reasoning (RPBA 2020, art.15(7)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence rules and practice
rubrics_metrics.description: EPC provides non‑exhaustive means of taking evidence (documents, witness hearings, expert opinions, inspection, sworn statements), but in practice documents predominate; expert opinions and witness hearings are rare because Technical Boards have technical judges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Witnesses are mainly used where public prior use is alleged and are often already heard at first instance; parties should plan evidence knowing Boards rely chiefly on documentary submissions (EPC art.117).

rubrics_metrics.name: Confidentiality and public file inspection
rubrics_metrics.description: Files may be inspected on request but parts are excluded from public inspection (e.g., documents relating to exclusion/objections to Board members, all draft decisions and internal preparatory documents, and medical certificates). Parties may request exclusion of documents prejudicial to legitimate personal or economic interests.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Boards may also exclude documents of their own motion to protect third‑party interests; the public part of the file is accessible via the European Patent Register (EPC arts.128(4), r.144; decisions on excluded documents referenced).

rubrics_metrics.name: Early case management: rapporteur and preliminary study
rubrics_metrics.description: The chair may designate only the rapporteur initially, who conducts a preliminary study of the appeal, assesses priority (e.g., likely remittal), suggests joinder with related appeals and identifies fundamental deficiencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only once the Board composition is complete may the rapporteur draft communications, prepare for oral proceedings and draft decisions (RPBA 2020, art.5).

rubrics_metrics.name: Acceleration of appeal proceedings
rubrics_metrics.description: A Board may accelerate proceedings of its own motion; parties or national courts may request acceleration and must provide reasons/evidence if a party requests it (courts need not give specific reasons).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Valid reasons include pending or envisaged national infringement proceedings or requests from licensees; accelerated cases may follow a strict case management timetable and shortened notice periods subject to fair hearing rights (RPBA 2020, art.10; EPC r.115).

rubrics_metrics.name: Annual list of cases for planning
rubrics_metrics.description: Each Board publishes an annual list, before the new calendar year, indicating cases likely to be treated in the coming year, particularly those where oral proceedings or communications are likely.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The list, prepared by chairs in October, aims to increase efficiency, transparency and predictability for Boards and parties (RPBA 2020, art.1(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Costs allocation and apportionment
rubrics_metrics.description: The default rule in inter partes proceedings is that each party bears its own costs; the Board may apportion costs differently for reasons of equity and upon request.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Eligible costs include those due to late amendments, obstructive behaviour or abuse of procedure; costs awarded must be necessarily and reasonably incurred. The Board may apportion by percentage or specify a sum; final cost orders are directly enforceable in Contracting States (EPC art.104; RPBA 2020, art.16).

rubrics_metrics.name: Public availability and timing of written communications
rubrics_metrics.description: Boards issue communications and preliminary opinions to help focus proceedings, usually issued at least four months before oral proceedings; most substantive communications come when the oral proceedings date is set.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some written communications can set time limits (e.g., Rule 100(2) communications) and failure to reply in ex parte cases can have severe consequences (e.g., deemed withdrawal) (EPC art.100(3); RPBA 2020 references).

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits on review and petitions for review (Article 112a)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Enlarged Board provides a limited judicial review of Boards’ decisions for fundamental procedural defects under Article 112a EPC; petitions for review are exceptional and the grounds are exhaustively defined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A successful petition sets aside the decision and reopens appeal proceedings; the Enlarged Board stressed Art.112a is not a mechanism to re‑decide substantive law (R 1/08 and related jurisprudence).
